newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Shell struggles to contain Nigeria oil dilemma.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Shell struggles to contain Nigeria oil dilemma.

text.p: Oil production for Shell in Nigeria is easy. Very little else is.

A year after the execution of author and minority rights campaigner Ken Saro-Wiwa at the hands of Nigeria's military rulers, the oil-rich swamps of the Niger river delta still present the Anglo-Dutch multinational with the knottiest of dilemmas.
What are its responsibilities in a developing country with few social services and little local infrastructure?
Shell is in Nigeria because the country supplies more crude than any other of its operations, has huge and easily extractable reserves and provides a clear profit of more than $220 million a year.
Ideally the company is keen to divide politics from economics but admits that on the ground it is not that simple, partly because it is seen as the only source of social amenities.
"We cannot completely assume the role of local government," said Egbert Imomoh, Shell's manager in Port Harcourt in the Bonny oilfields east of the Niger.
"Because these oil producing areas lack the basic infrastructure, we are being called upon to do much more than should be expected of the corporate citizen."

Saro-Wiwa and eight other activists from the Movement for the Survival of the Ogoni Peoples (MOSOP) were campaigning for Ogoni rights and compensation from Shell at the heart of its hugely profitable delta operations.
MOSOP supporters in the West condemned Shell for not doing more to intervene on Saro-Wiwa's behalf.
Scores more rural communities across the delta target Shell, accusing the company of environmental damage and stealing their birthright.
But the underlying issue for the tribesmen living next to Shell since oil started flowing in 1958, that of simple living standards, has barely been addressed.
PROBLEM IS DISPARITY OF WEALTH

"The root of the problem is inequity in distribution of wealth," said Victor Dania, Public and Community Affairs Manager for Shell east of the Niger. "Community leaders accept that. They tell us they're using Shell to attract the attention of the government."
"We will always ask Shell to do more," said Chief Gana Manuwa, chairman of the Delta Oil Producing Communities Association.
"Facilities are appalling and Shell is our immediate neighbour. We see little sign of the government."
Living standards across the Niger swamplands have slumped. Traditional farming and fishing are in terminal decline.
"We have no water, no roads, no electricity, no telephones. Hospitals and schools are disintegrating. Our fear is that when the oil runs dry we could be left with nothing," said Chief Manuwa.
The government, which relies on oil exports for 90 percent of foreign change revenues, has failed to redistribute multi-billion dollar annual earnings to its people.

The state oil company NNPC is struggling to finance its 55 percent share in the joint venture consortium run by Shell, running up huge debts, and has been accused of scuppering new developments and denying funds to smooth community relations.

"This country has got it all back to front," said Steve Ollerearnshaw, in charge of operations in the oil town of Warri in the Forcados oilfields west of the Niger. "The government is in the oil business and the oil industry is in local government."
Shell, caught in the middle, admits that until recently it did not do enough to contain growing resentment among the communities which flared into violence in 1993 and 1994.
The company fled Ogoniland in the eastern delta in 1993 amid sabotage and attacks on its staff. In the west, a three day siege of Shell's Warri compound brought executives to the negotiating table.
"I don't think we did enough," said Brian Anderson, Shell's managing director in Nigeria. "At the time we could have done a bit more and we didn't, but now I think we're doing what we have to."

"Shell had a reputation for being technically good but somewhat arrogant," admitted Ollerearnshaw. "I think we've made a real effort in the last two years to get close to the community. Things are definitely improving."
Shell's spending on community assistance, to schools, hospitals and the like has risen sharply in the past two years.
Community spending increased to $30 million this year with another $90 million spent on the environment.
The company says it easily outspends the government in the delta. As a result, oil production lost to sabotage and other community disturbances has been reduced sharply from its peak in 1994.
Local leaders say they forced Shell to act and that without any semblance of local government the company, after nearly 50 years in the country, must do more.
"Shell provides a top-up budget," said Francis Chukwu, a doctor at a Shell supported cottage hospital in Egbema, Rivers State. "But it is peanuts. We need more."
SELLING STATE'S OIL ASSETS IS THE ANSWER, SHELL SAYS
Shell is pinning its hopes on embryonic government plans for divesting state-owned oil assets.
Anderson says this is the only option for getting the debt-ridden oil sector back on track while providing a huge cash injection for the fragile Nigerian economy.
"It is an opportunity for them, if the cash is used wisely to diversify the economy and improve the general infrastructure," he said.
If the economic cake is not re-distributed Shell could be in for more trouble.

"If the economy improves then...I believe we can handle the community issues," said Imomoh in Port Harcourt. "But if the macro economic climate does not improve then...I can't say how we will manage that situation."
